idea-plugin.name: Flowable Atlas
idea-plugin.description:
The complete Flowable companion for IntelliJ IDEA. Flowable Atlas turns the model keys and expressions scattered across your Java code and Flowable models into first-class, IDE-aware references — completed, validated and navigable — and maps your whole project into a single interactive explorer. Everything is resolved against the models that actually live in your repository, so a wrong key or a broken expression is caught in the editor, long before deployment.

Zero configuration: open a project that contains the Flowable models you exported from Design (the app .zip / deployment -bar, holding .bpmn / .cmmn / .dmn / .form / .data / .service / …) or the Flowable Design *-models workspace, and start typing. The plugin indexes every model and puts that knowledge to work across three areas.

1 · Model-key intelligence

  • Context-aware key completion at every Flowable API position that takes a model key — process, case, decision, form, event, channel, data object, master data, service, action, agent, knowledge base, template, security policy, query, variable extractor, sequence, SLA, dashboard component, data dictionary, page and unified work definitions. Both org.flowable.* and com.flowable.*. Search by key, by name, or by any fragment — type 0061 to get DEMO-DO-0061.
  • Cascade completion for fluent chains — operation("…") completes the operations of the data object / service resolved from the sibling definitionKey(…) / serviceKey(…) (constant references are resolved), and value("…", …) completes that operation's input fields. DMN variable("…", …) offers the decision's input/output variables.
  • More than keys — completion for message & signal names, process variables, task-definition keys and activity IDs, scoped to the processDefinitionKey / caseDefinitionKey in the same query chain when present, so you see only that model's ids.
  • Model → model references in BPMN/CMMN XML — the keys that live inside the models themselves (callActivity calledElement, flowable:formKey, decisionRef, CMMN caseRef / processRef) get the same completion, Ctrl/Cmd-click navigation and broken-key inspection as Java call sites — so a calledElement pointing at a missing process is caught before deployment.
  • Broken-key inspection — an unknown key (in Java or model XML) is flagged inline with a "did you mean …?" quick-fix to the closest real key.
  • Navigation & Find Usages — Ctrl/Cmd-click a key literal to jump straight to the model file; hover for its type, name and location. Find Usages on a delegate class or an ${bean.method()} expression lists the model files that reference it.
  • Code generation — generate a typed Java constants class (FlowableModelKeys.Process.ORDER_FULFILMENT, model name in Javadoc) that stays in sync as models are added, renamed or removed; or, with Alt/Option-Enter on a data-object definitionKey("…"), a typed Java bean built from the model's field mappings.
  • Liquibase aware — inside a changelog it completes <column> names and tableName from the backing service model, and flags columns that no backing Flowable model defines.

2 · Flowable expression language support

  • Both dialects, first-class — the backend JUEL dialect (${…} / #{…}) and the frontend form dialect ({{…}}) each get syntax highlighting, rainbow parentheses and brace matching.
  • Live validation — structural syntax errors, and unknown functions, namespaces or flw.* members, are flagged against a catalog of the real, verified Flowable function set.
  • Expression completion — functions, engine root objects, and your project's own process/case variables and form fields.
  • Recognised inline, everywhere expressions live — BPMN/CMMN/DMN XML, .form / .page JSON, and (optionally) Java string literals — so the highlighting, validation and completion follow you into the models you edit.
  • Real Groovy & JavaScript in script bodies — BPMN/CMMN script tasks, listener scripts and action-bot scripts get the IDE's own language support injected inline: compiler-grade syntax errors, highlighting and fragment editing (Alt-Enter). Groovy is bundled in every IDEA; JavaScript lights up on Ultimate. JUEL or unknown script formats keep the plain expression injection. Atlas additionally runs its own dependency-free structural script check (unterminated strings/comments, unbalanced brackets, scriptFormat typos) in the CLI and the explorer's Checks tab.
  • Flowable environments — define your DEV/QA/UAT/PROD servers once for the whole IDE instead of once per repository, and pick them from a list. Each environment holds a Flowable Design connection, a Flowable Work connection, or just one of the two; the Design pull and the Atlas Playground point independently, so running against QA while models still come from DEV1 is an ordinary way to work. Mark an environment Protected and Atlas asks before pulling from it or evaluating against it. Passwords and tokens stay in the IDE password safe.
  • Atlas Playground (a tool window) — type an expression, pick backend or frontend, and get instant validation and completion; scope completion to one model; evaluate a frontend expression live against a pasted JSON payload; or evaluate a backend expression against a running app through the Flowable Inspect REST API. Which app it runs against is one of your environments, and the fastest way to switch is to paste a Work URL: the environment, the scope and the instance id all fill in from the link.
  • Script Playground (the Scripts tab of the same tool window) — paste or write a Groovy/JavaScript/Python script: the IDE's real language editing (completion, coloring) where the language plugin is available, live structural validation with squiggles and clickable problem rows (the same checks the CLI and the explorer's Checks tab run), the scope variables the script touches as chips, a picker that loads any script task / listener / action-bot script straight from the project's models, and a library of worked examples — a complete, commented script for every context and language, to start from rather than from an empty editor.

3 · Atlas explorer & hub

  • Atlas Hub — a tool window (right stripe) that is the plugin's control center: which Flowable project Atlas is about, how many models it knows and how fresh that is, one attention line when something needs a hand, and three task blocks — the generated explorer, the Flowable Design pull, the playground's runtime — each with its actions beside its state, kept up to date live.
  • Map your whole project — Tools → Flowable Atlas → Generate Atlas Explorer… turns your models + Java + Liquibase into a single self-contained, offline, interactive HTML page. Save it into the project and open it in your browser or right inside the IDE (embedded viewer), then click through every relationship in both directions. In Settings → Generation you pick exactly which artifacts are written — summary & overview Markdown, the graph JSON, the explorer HTML, a CLAUDE.md primer for AI agents, and a Playwright guide that lets an agent drive Flowable Work in a browser, with this project's stage bars, tasks, required fields and button conditions. Generation runs entirely in-process — no external tools required — and honours the project's expression allowlist.
  • An ER diagram designer — tick ER diagram designer (HTML) under Settings → Generation and Atlas writes a page of its own beside the explorer: drag the project's tables onto a canvas, show their columns and types, search across every table and column, draw named 1:1 / 1:n / n:m relations, colour them and let Atlas arrange them — for explaining a data model to the business — with SVG/PNG export and a diagram file you can commit; Tools → Flowable Atlas opens it in an editor tab in the IDE's theme. It carries only the tables, so it stays small however large the project is.
  • IDE-native viewing — the embedded explorer follows the IDE light/dark theme (switching restyles live) and carries a toolbar with Regenerate Atlas Explorer, Reload, Open Atlas Playground and Open in Browser.
  • Reopen without regenerating — Open Atlas Explorer (Atlas Hub, or Tools → Flowable Atlas) opens an already-generated *.explorer.html — including one written by the standalone atlas CLI into the configured output folder — as a center editor tab (like a DB table), so you never have to leave the IDE for a browser.

How it feels

  • runtimeService.startProcessInstanceByKey("<caret>") → your process keys.
  • cmmnRuntimeService.createCaseInstanceBuilder().caseDefinitionKey("<caret>") → your case keys.
  • dataObjectRuntimeService.createDataObjectInstanceQuery().definitionKey(KEY).operation("<caret>") → that data object's operations; .value("<caret>", …) → the operation's fields.
  • Press completion twice to list all model keys of every type, regardless of the call site.

Completion fires inside string literals and at bare arguments alike (inserting a quoted key), with Flowable keys ranked to the top — no setup beyond opening a project that contains your Flowable models.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.30.1

  • graph.json is back to its size on projects with large, nested forms. 0.30.0 copied the gated containers around a form field — each panel or subform that can hide, disable or ignore it, with its conditions — onto every field inside them. That grew with fields × nesting depth × condition length, and on large, deeply nested forms it multiplied the size of the whole graph and slowed the explorer and everything else that reads it. A form now describes each such container once, under containers, and a field's containerGates lists only their ids, nearest first.

0.30.0

  • A guide for agents that drive Flowable Work in a browser. Atlas now writes <project>.playwright.md: what an agent with a browser — the Playwright MCP server, a Playwright script or another browser tool — needs to work in Work rather than on the code. Start a case or process, open a case or task, see which stage a case is in, claim and complete tasks and fill in their forms, press a case's actions, bring a case to a given stage, find the open tasks of a user or group, explain why a button is missing or greyed out, and know when to stop and ask. The first part is how Work behaves, for any project: a quick start that reads a case's whole state in one call; the rules (act through the UI, only look through REST, never click a disabled button, ask before anything irreversible); the sign-in, the routes, Create New, the stage bar, the toolbar where manual-activation items and user event listeners become buttons, and a task's outcome buttons; the read-only REST endpoints that explain a screen; the CMMN rules that move a case; a checklist for a disabled button; the loop for reaching a stage; and the Playwright traps, with what each script call is in Playwright MCP.
  • The guide says which Work it describes. Locators, dialogs and buttons differ between Work's lines. The guide describes 2026.1 and newer, marks what older lines do differently, and keeps a table with one column each for 2026.1 and newer, 2025.2, 2025.1 with 3.15–3.17, and 3.14 and older — apart because Work's own screens got their ARIA roles only in 3.15. The version the project builds against names the column, and the agent is told to read the running version from the system before relying on it. The notes were compiled from Work's frontend source for each line and its own end-to-end test helpers, not by driving a running Work; the guide says so, and what to fall back on when a locator finds nothing.
  • Its second part is this project, read from its models. An index of every deployed case and process: its key, the link that starts it (#/work?create=true&definitionKey=<key>, which also tells apart two definitions with one title), its stage bar or its number of user tasks, and who may start it; then the apps the sidebar shows, with their pages. Behind the index, for each case: its stage bar in Work's order, and for each stage what starts it, read out of its sentries, whether it completes by itself, and the tasks, manual items and listeners inside it with the groups that get them. For each process: its user tasks in flow order and what leads to each. For every form: its required fields and their validation rules, its outcomes and the variable they write, and its conditional buttons. A condition on a variable names the outcome or the field that sets it, and ⚠ marks the traps: a required field that can be hidden, which, on a form saved by Design 3.8 or later, keeps the outcomes disabled with no error on the page, and stage-bar entries that share a displayOrder or have none, which Work reorders as they end. Models that only a test source set deploys are left out.
  • One artifact in two files. A skill is loaded whole, and on a real project the details are most of the text, so --all, the launcher and the plugin write them to a project map beside the guide, <project>.playwright-map.md, which its index points into; --playwright alone writes one file with the details inline. In the plugin, tick Playwright guide for Flowable Work (+ project map) under Settings → Tools → Flowable Atlas → Generation. The guide opens with skill front matter: copy it to .claude/skills/flowable-work-ui/SKILL.md and the map beside it as project-map.md, and Claude Code loads it when a request is about Work. With the guide written beside it, the generated CLAUDE.md names the requests it is for and says to read it before the first click. Written outside the project — the launcher's default — the guide names the map and the graph by their full path, the home directory as ~.
  • A sentry's condition is read from its ifPart. Design writes its condition builder as <flowable:condition> elements before the ifPart. Atlas took the first of them, which is empty, so on every sentry built that way the real condition was missing from the overview, the explorer and the graph.
  • The graph keeps what moves a case in Work. Sentries keep their triggerMode and the event each on-part waits for, and every entry and exit criterion the plan item it sits on (planItemId); an exit keeps its exitEventType and exitType. A case keeps its own exit criteria, its start form, its Work form and its candidate starter users. Stages and milestones keep displayOrder, includeInStageOverview and their place in Work's stage overview, and a stage its autoCompleteCondition. A plan item keeps the button name, groups and users of its manual activation, the start form that button opens, its maxInstanceCount and the collection a repetition runs over, and its parentCompletionRule and completionNeutralRule; a listener keeps its availableCondition, its timer, and the variable or signal it waits for. A user task keeps its candidate users and the sub-process around it, a multi-instance its completion condition, and a process its candidate starter users.
  • Forms and apps keep what Work shows of them. A form keeps the variable its outcome is stored in (outcomeVariableName), doNotCreateOutcomeVariable and the Design version it records. An outcome keeps visible, enabled, ignoreValidation and navigationUrl. A field keeps its validation rules — pattern, bounds, length, date format, custom checks — and the containers around it that can hide, disable or ignore it. An app keeps flowApp, its url and order, and each page its label and url.
  • A deployed model wins over its test copy. A model under a test source set (src/test/…) that shared its key with one the app deploys could stand in for it everywhere: the first copy read was the model, and loose files are read before archives, so an empty test fixture replaced the process a .bar deploys — in the explorer, the overview, the graph and the findings. Test copies are read last now: the deployed copy is the model, and a test copy that references other models is listed among its other copies.
  • A case's generic event listeners are among its event listeners. Design writes a variable, signal or reactivation listener as a generic eventListener, which Atlas did not count as one, so a signal listener was never linked to the models that throw its signal. It is listed now, with its kind, and linked.
  • A form input without a caption is a field. Design lets a modeller leave the label out, and such an input was never recorded: a task form whose only input was a required number field read as having nothing required. An input without a caption now counts when it is required, or bound to a value.
  • An app that lists its pages under pages contains them. Older Design workspace exports keep an app's pages there rather than under pageModels, the only place Atlas looked: such an app contained no page, and its pages' permissions were missing from the access map.
  • CLAUDE.md states the Flowable version of Work projects. Only engine versions (6.x–9.x) were accepted, and the property the platform's project template declares, <com.flowable.platform.version>, was not looked for: every Work project measured (3.11 to 2025.1) was told nothing about its version. Platform versions (3.x, 2025.x, 2026.x) are now found in Maven properties and dependencies and in Gradle properties, version catalogs and dependency coordinates, the platform's com.flowable.platform:… sub-groups included, and a platform version wins over an engine one. The Playwright guide picks its version column from it.
  • Execution order holds across a loop. When a process's flows loop back, the overview could put a step the loop leads to ahead of the loop's own gateway: breaking the cycle compared one step's position in the file with the order in which the walk had reached the others. The step the walk is waiting on goes first now, in the overview and in the guide's user tasks.
  • A project given as . names its files by its directory. Run on . from inside the project, the summary, the overview and CLAUDE.md pointed at ..graph.json, ..overview.md and so on, while the files themselves were written under the directory's name. They name the files as written now.
  • The Atlas Hub stays where you scrolled it. Ticking or unticking an app in the Design block threw the panel back up to the Explorer block, so the next app further down meant scrolling down again — and so did every other refresh of the Hub: an analysis landing, or the index rebuilt. The Hub now keeps its place.

0.29.0

  • A button that would wipe the form is a finding. An expression button stores what it computes, and a REST button what its call returns, in the variable its value binds — but only a plain binding names one. {{}}, {{ }}, an expression such as {{a + b}}, a literal or no value at all binds no path, and the forms runtime then writes the result over the form's whole payload, or a bound panel's whole value: every field the user filled in is gone the moment the button is pressed, or the moment the form opens when it runs on its own. The new defect payloadOverwrite names each such button by Design's name and its id, says what its value is and whether it runs on its own, shows the value as the finding's snippet and opens on the button. A REST button that maps its response with Store response attributes writes the mapped names instead and is not reported. Atlas now runs twenty-five checks.
  • Elements: Design's palette, turned round. A new page, #/elements (sidebar → Models → Elements), lists the palette entries the project's processes, cases, forms and pages use, each with how often, under Design's own groups and in its order — start events, activities, gateways … for processes, tasks, sentries, listeners for cases, data entry, selection, display, container, Flowable Work for forms and pages. Pick one and the page lists every model holding it, opened to the elements themselves: caption, id, the value a form component binds or stores, and any open finding on it, each a click away from the element in its model. The filter narrows by element id, caption, value, model name, key or file, and the pick and the filter ride in the URL.
  • Every form component is called what Design calls it. A form's Fields table, the Elements page and the search name all of the form and page palette by Design's word: an upload is an Attachment, a htmlComponent a Text display, a number with numberType float a Decimal, a select with multi a Select (multiple) — the parser now records which of the two entries sharing a type a component came from. Document tasks (Create document, Merge documents, PDF convert) and the other Flowable Work tasks have their Design names too.
  • The search asks for elements by type. has:attachment, has:"start event", has:"expression button" or has:scriptButton finds the models holding an element of that type, by the type the model stores or by Design's word for it. Beside has:, id: and label: describe that same element: has:attachment label:passport is the form with an attachment captioned Passport. The row names the element that matched and opens on it; the Elements page hands its pick to the search with one click.
  • A word of punctuation only is searched for as written. {{}}, ${} or => split into no words at all, so the query was empty and the palette answered with the recent list. Such a word is now matched literally: {{}} finds every empty binding and every form whose button stores its result in one.

0.28.8

  • An endpoint's page says what it takes. A REST endpoint's page named its path, its handler and who calls it, but not what a caller has to send. Its Overview now opens with Parameters: every {variable} of the path, then each query parameter, header, cookie, multipart part and the body its handler declares (@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestHeader, @CookieValue, @RequestPart, @RequestBody). Each row shows the name the caller sends, the type, whether it is required and its default, for Java and Kotlin handlers alike. Required follows Spring: required = false, a defaultValue, an Optional or a Kotlin T? makes a parameter optional. A parameter without an annotation is listed as the query parameter Spring binds it to. What the server supplies itself (the request, the principal, a session attribute) is not listed. A path variable the handler takes but the path does not name is marked not in the path, since Spring fails every such request, and a handler that takes nothing says so. A class's Endpoints served now links each path to its page, and graph.json carries the same list as the endpoint's params.
  • A handler behind a nested annotation has its own name again. When a mapping was followed by @PreAuthorize("hasRole('A')"), or by an OpenAPI @Operation(…) with annotations nested inside it, the handler was named after a word inside that annotation (hasRole) instead of the method.

0.28.7

  • The ER designer takes databases and tables of your own. A data model rarely ends at the project's schema — an order refers to a customer kept in a CRM, a task to an engine table no changelog creates. The table list is now grouped by database: the project's own first, then every database added with + Database. + Table on a group adds a table by hand — a name, and a row per column with its type and whether it is the primary key — to that database or to the project's own. A table added by hand is a table like any other: it relates to any table of any database, frames, arranges and searches, and its panel edits it; a renamed table or column keeps its relations. The databases belong to the diagram and its file (format version 4). Every card names its database, small in its corner.
  • A diagram kept in the project exports again, and says when it was changed. Opened for the first time in a browser, the diagram was the very object it was compared with: changed here never showed, and an export of it — the diagram file, SVG or PNG — failed without a word.
  • The ER designer's search finds tables again. It ranked what the diagram already shows before everything else, tables and columns alike, so the columns of the tables on the canvas came first — an order_id_ in each of them buried the ORDER table, and past sixty rows it was not listed at all, though the count above the list said it was found. Tables now come first, then columns; within each, what the diagram shows first, as before. And what a search finds in a table's name is marked on its card, as a column it finds is — and in the list, what its filter finds.

0.28.6

  • An ER designer relation meets the rows of the columns it joins. Over several columns it left the card from halfway between their rows — over id_ and total_, from customer_id_, a row it does not join. Now it forks just outside the card, a short stub with a dot to each of its rows. A relation over columns also meets them when the two cards stand one above the other — from the side, as a bow, where it used to run from edge to edge past every column — and a folded card shows the columns its relations join, in their place among its first five, where a column beyond them left the line at the card's header. A relation without columns meets the card's middle, as before.

0.28.5

  • An ER designer relation can join on several columns. The relation's panel lists the columns it joins, a row per pair under the two tables' names, and + Column pair adds one — for a key over several columns, order_id_, line_no_ → order_id_, line_no_, paired position by position as SQL pairs them. The line leaves each card from between its columns' rows. In the diagram file, fromColumn and toColumn are a name each for one column and lists for several; the file is version 3, so 0.28.4 refuses it rather than read the relations without their columns.
  • Every relation the models state is proposed, not one per pair of tables. Two fields of one data object that both refer to a customer — a buyer and a payer — were one proposal, and taking it hid the other. Now each is proposed on its own, over the columns it joins: a service's column relation joins exactly its column and the one it refers to, and a data object field the columns its service maps it to. When a data object and its service tell the same relation it is one proposal, named as the data object names it and counted as the service counts it. A relation you draw accounts for the proposal over its columns — else the first one left — and leaves the others.

0.28.4

  • The ER designer's relations say how many at each end. A relation had four cardinalities — 1:1, 1:n, n:1, n:m — and none of them could say that a customer may have no orders at all, or an order at most one invoice. Now each end is chosen on its own, a row each in the relation's panel: 1 exactly one, 0..1 zero or one, 1..n one or more, 0..n zero or more — the minimum and maximum crow's-foot notation draws, so the two rows give all sixteen cardinalities, 0..n:1, 1:0..1, 0..n:0..n and the rest. The line draws them as the notation does — a ring for none, a bar for one, a foot for many — with the count beside it, and the sentence under the choice says what it means (Many to one: each Order has exactly one Customer, each Customer zero or more Order). ⇄ now turns a relation round with each table keeping its own end, where it used to hand the ends to the other table.
  • Frames gather tables under a name. Frame in the designer's toolbar (or F), then drag over the tables: the frame holds whatever lies inside it, gets a name and a colour in its panel, moves with its tables when dragged by its name tab or edge, and resizes by its corners; Fit to its tables draws it around them again. Arrange keeps a frame's tables together, arranged inside it, and places the frame as one block beside what its tables relate to. Frames are in exported pictures and in the diagram file.
  • The diagram file is version 2, for the frames and the counts at each end. A version 1 file reads as it is (1:n is 1:0..n, n:m is 0..n:0..n); 0.28.3 and older refuse a version 2 file rather than read it without its frames.

0.28.3

  • A large project's explorer is a fraction of its size, and opens under Remote Development again. 0.28.0 made the explorer carry every Liquibase column's origin, every change set and each service's schema coverage — on the projects measured the Liquibase part of the page about tripled — and a large project's explorer grew past 20 MB: the IDE's content limit, above which a Remote Development client refuses to open a file (the file is too large) before any editor is asked. The graph inside the page, above 1 MB, is now embedded deflated and inflated by the page itself before it starts. It deflates about tenfold, so an explorer is about a quarter of its size (5.4 MB to 1.4 MB on the largest project measured) and still one self-contained HTML file that opens the same way in any browser, from disk, from a web server or in the IDE. Nothing on the page changes.
  • The ER designer's table list can be dragged wider, for a table name longer than the list: drag its right edge, or move the focused edge with ← →; a double click or Home resets it. The width is remembered in this browser.

0.28.2

  • The ER diagram designer is a page of its own: <project>.erd.html. It was a page inside the explorer, and that was the wrong place: the explorer carries the whole graph, and a large one outgrows what a Remote Development client will open, while the designer needs a sliver of it. The new page carries only the tables — the Liquibase changelogs' columns, the database services, the data objects that read a table and their relations — and the project's *.atlas-erd.json diagrams, so it stays a few hundred KB however large the project is. --all writes it beside the explorer when the project has a table, its tables linking into the explorer's pages; --erd writes it on its own. In the plugin it is the artifact ER diagram designer (HTML) in Settings → Generation, and opens in the same kind of editor tab, whose Regenerate rewrites it and whose banner says when the models are newer. The explorer is back to what it was before the designer: no --extension flag, no Explorer extensions setting, no #/erd page (a link to one opens the overview). On the corpora measured, the designer was about 100 KB of an explorer; a page of 20 MB is the project's own data, which the explorer carries as before.
  • Search every table and column. ⌘F, Ctrl+F or / in the designer searches the project's tables and their columns — by name, business name, data object or column type — on the diagram or not. The results list tables and table.column rows, the diagram's own first; Enter goes to one, centred on the column, and adds its table when the diagram does not have it. While a search is on, matching cards are outlined, the rest step back, matching columns are marked, and a folded card also shows the columns it found — the one column of forty without unfolding the rest. A table's panel filters its columns too.
  • Expand all, collapse all. Two buttons unfold every card to all its columns and fold them back to the first five, one undo step each; unfolding moves the cards below down so none is covered.
  • A table's data object and service keys, to copy. An (i) beside the table's name in its panel unfolds what is behind it — its changelog, the services that map it and the data objects that read it — each name with its key under it and a copy button, and the table's own name has a copy button in the panel's title; the line that listed them under forty columns, out of sight, is gone. In the list, a table read by one data object has a quiet copy icon for that key beside the data object's name, and the same (i), before the table is on the canvas. A search finds a table by those keys too.
  • The ER diagram from the menu. With ER diagram designer (HTML) chosen in Settings → Generation, Tools → Flowable Atlas — and so the Atlas Hub's ⋮ — has an Open Atlas ER Diagram Designer: it opens the newest page in an editor tab, generating one into the output folder first when there is none. In the IDE the page wears the IDE's theme and colours exactly as the explorer does — it runs the explorer's own theme code — and its toolbar keeps to one row in a narrow editor tab.

0.28.1

  • The ER diagram designer arranges the tables for you. Arrange in the designer's toolbar lays every table out by its relations — for a diagram with too many tables to sort by hand: each relation's one side in a column left of its many side, the tables in a column ordered so that as few relation lines cross as possible, each table level with the ones it relates to, the columns far enough apart for the relation names between them, and unrelated tables and separate groups packed underneath. The cards glide to their places and one undo puts them back.
  • Relation names no longer sit on top of each other. Two relations whose lines meet in the same gap drew their names in one place; the lower one now moves below the upper, on the canvas and in an exported picture alike.

0.28.0

  • An ER diagram designer in the explorer, for explaining a data model. A page generated with --extension erd has an ER diagram entry: the project's tables in a list — every table the Liquibase changelogs leave once they have run, with each column's type as written, and the tables of database services no changelog creates — to drag onto a canvas. A card shows a table's business name, its table name and its first five columns, unfolds to all of them, and takes a colour; columns can be dragged into the order that decides which five show. Drawing from a card's dot to another table makes a relation with a name and a cardinality (1:1, 1:n, n:1, n:m), drawn with crow's feet, and the relations the models already state — a data object field referring to another data object, a service column relation — are offered as dashed proposals to take with one click. Undo and redo, several diagrams per project, a Present mode that shows the diagram and nothing else, and SVG and PNG export for a slide. What you draw is kept in the browser, per project.
  • Explorer extensions are optional, and absent unless chosen. The designer is the first explorer extension: its code is inlined only into a page generated with it (--extension on the CLI, comma-separated), so a page without it is byte-for-byte what it was, and a #/erd link opened there lands on the overview. An unknown extension, or --extension with an output that has no explorer page, is a misuse (exit 2).
  • A diagram can live in the project. Export → Diagram file writes <name>.atlas-erd.json, which imports again in any explorer — from the menu, by dropping it on the canvas, or by pasting it in the IDE. Commit it anywhere in the project and every explorer generated with the designer opens on it without an import; what someone changes there stays in their browser, marked changed here, until they export it again. A diagram refers to tables by name, so it follows the schema: a dropped column leaves its card, a new one joins, and a table the project no longer has is drawn dashed from the diagram's own snapshot.
  • A changelog's primary key is known. Atlas reads which columns are a table's primary key — an inline <constraints primaryKey="true"/>, <addPrimaryKey>, PRIMARY KEY in formatted SQL or an <sql> block — and keeps it through a rename and drops it with <dropPrimaryKey>. A changelog's page tags those columns PK, and the ER diagram designer marks them with a key and lists them first on a card.
  • The plugin chooses the explorer's extensions per project. Settings → Tools → Flowable Atlas → Generation → Explorer extensions has a checkbox per extension, stored with the project's other generation settings. Changing it regenerates the explorer, so the page on disk has the designer — or loses it — at once; with no page yet, the IDE offers to generate one. Inside the IDE's explorer tab the designer works, and Export copies the diagram file or the SVG to the clipboard, since the tab cannot download.

0.27.2

  • Liquibase changelogs are replayed the way Liquibase runs them, and a table shows what it holds at the end. Changelogs were matched with regular expressions and deduplicated by file name, so of a history kept as v2/customer.xml, v3/customer.xml and v4/customer.xml only the first file was read, and the table showed what that one said. Atlas now reads the XML itself and follows a master's <include> and <includeAll> where they stand, an includeAll in Liquibase's plain path order. A change set is identified by its id, author and logicalFilePath, so one that already ran does not run again. A failed precondition skips its change set, a <rollback> or a commented-out change set no longer adds or drops anything, and <sql>, <sqlFile> and formatted-SQL changelogs have their DDL read. Every copy of one schema definition — the same app exported into several folders — is one history too.
  • A service's table is the one the application builds. When a project keeps its tables in its own changelogs, run by the application at startup, and the app carries the schema definition the service model names, Atlas read the definition. The columns the project added in its own changelog were then reported as "not in Liquibase", and the project's changelog as superseded by its older copy in the app. The application's changelog now describes the table. A definition with the same logicalFilePath as the application's changelog is marked copy, not superseded. Changelogs of one Liquibase run never supersede one another: the file that adds a column to another file's table is part of that table. On a real project this took the changelog findings from 15 to 3, the three definitions the project really had left behind.
  • A changelog the application uses for its own tables is no orphan. An application changelog that names no service, and whose tables no service maps, backs a table the code owns — a JPA entity, a lock table — and is no longer reported. One that names a service the project does not define still is, and the finding now says which service.
  • A changelog page shows its change sets and where each column came from. The explorer lists every change set in run order with what it changes and whether it ran, was skipped by its precondition, or had already run from another file. Each column names the change set that added it, and a column or table a later change set dropped or renamed is listed as gone. In the schema coverage table, a mapped column the table no longer has says which change set dropped or renamed it, where it said "not in changelog".
  • The IDE's changelog inspection knows about the project's other changelogs. Liquibase column not defined in Flowable model flagged a column at its declaration even when a later changelog dropped or renamed it, as a v3/ folder does to a v2/ one. It now replays the project's changelogs and leaves a column alone once the table no longer has it.
  • New check: an app's copy of a changelog that differs from the code. A schema definition that shares its logicalFilePath with one of the application's changelogs is a copy of it. changelogDrift compares the two change set by change set, setting whitespace, attribute order and comments aside. When they differ, one sentence names both files and the change sets that are only in the code, only in the app, or different. On a real project, 11 of 12 such copies differed: an index, a column or a changed type that only one side had.
  • A changelog that is not well-formed XML is reported. Liquibase stops at startup on a changelog it cannot read; Atlas reported nothing and read what its regular expressions found. It is now a parse issue.

Older releases: see CHANGELOG.md in the repository.
